nit: `libocp-ami` ?
Acknowledged

I don't really know how OCP releases specs, but we're going to base code on a "pre-1.0" spec?

What is the plan for future iterations of the spec + code?  I would like some words listed here as to the expected policy when it comes to implementation proposals out of draft specs.

Writing code against draft specs in open source is potentially problematic; we need to have a consensus on the approach to be taken here.

- Not everyone is a member of OCP and has access to draft specs.  This means we can end up with code proposals that public reviewers cannot confirm in any way.
- Adding APIs for draft specs means we end up with "users".  If those draft specs do not make their way to publish state, we've effectively forked the spec.

This is a great question! Yes, I need to add some text to make this clear.

The v1 spec is actually public now (https://www.opencompute.org/documents/ocp-gpu-accelerator-management-interfaces-v1-pdf), will update this doc.

As you see in the v1 spec (section 3.6), there are 2 ways to compose request messages (and responses) by device vendors in order to be compliant with the OCP spec - PCIe ID based and IANA based. Further, you can see that the command code itself can be vendor specific. Of course, there is the option to define certain command codes in the OCP spec itself and have the IANA set to OCP itself - this would be useful to avoid duplication of work to define commands for telemetry that are common to multiple vendors.

What this means is: the code in this repo will correspond to either a public release of the OCP base spec or the public release of an OCP base spec compliant vendor spec (in which case the code could reside in a vendor/<company> directory).

> or the public release of an OCP base spec compliant vendor spec (in which case the code could reside in a vendor/<company> directory).

This is a very big leap that isn't talked about at all in this document.
Agree, I will add it in a prominent way in the doc.
Acknowledged
So we're implementing one particular section of a higher-level spec?  Why is the library proposed to be named after the entire spec?

We're doing that, and in addition there would be vendor sections (see my comment elsewhere). Those vendor specs are still OCP compliant, so I don't think we have an issue naming the repo as libocp-ami.

We need words written about vendor specs here then.  There is nothing currently written that implies we're going to open this up to vendor specs.

I'm relatively concerned that this just becomes a dumping ground for Nvidia to make up all sorts of OEM commands that aren't even interesting to OpenBMC (or are at least never tied to any upstream daemons) just because "they exist" in your hardware.

I will add text for this in the next doc. Will push in a day or so.

One of the main purpose of adding this to OpenBMC is to let OpenBMC daemons consume this - we will be pushing patches for that as well.

> I'm relatively concerned that this just becomes a dumping ground for Nvidia to make up all sorts of OEM commands that aren't even interesting to OpenBMC (or are at least never tied to any upstream daemons) just because "they exist" in your hardware.

This is partly why I have the ABI controls in libpldm, and require that another open source project needs to use the symbols before they can be marked stable. From there, anything that is marked testing can be reworked as anyone sees fit, and we aren't burdened too much by maintenance. At the same time, the code exists in-tree and can be exploited by those that need it, which I hope encourages people to contribute.
This is a good approach and we can do the same. Added as a requirement.
Acknowledged
Where is this expressed?  Anonymous "desires" aren't really a great way to base our code policy around.

I will reword to indicate this as a design element for this library.

What I noted is based on discussions Nvidia has had internally and with several customers and industry partners - most don't want to rewrite the protocol library part, even on device firmware and non-OpenBMC BMC firmware stacks.

> What I noted is based on discussions Nvidia has had internally and with several customers and industry partners - most don't want to rewrite the protocol library part, even on device firmware and non-OpenBMC BMC firmware stacks.

While this might be interesting to Nvidia, you're asking the open source community to take on a burden for **your customers**.  We need to quantify that burden.  Why should the OpenBMC community do extra work to make non-OpenBMC (ie. proprietary) BMC firmware stacks easier?  "device firmware" is ... your devices; so I'm having trouble understanding how this is an "industry ask".

libcper was [Open]BMC + BIOS.  That makes a lot more sense to me than OpenBMC + proprietary BMCs.

Is anyone from AMD interested in collaborating on this library?  Is anyone making a custom ML training chip interested in collaborating?  If not, this is just Nvidia?

I mentioned this above about vendor support, but I'd be much more comfortable with this if there is true industry interest in collaborating here (partially because the "competitors" can better help keep the code in line with community expectations).  We've had enough history with vendor-specific playgrounds in this community that I don't want to encourage new ones.

In terms of device vendors - Nvidia and AMD are interested.

CSPs (MSFT, Meta, Google) are interested because they wouldn't want Nvidia/AMD/device vendors to provide different APIs for common telemetry access.

The companies I mentioned above have representatives in the OCP WG that produced this spec (their names are also in the spec). Please let me know how you'd want me to call this out in the doc.

> In terms of device vendors - Nvidia and AMD are interested.

Let's get someone from AMD to step up and be a contributor then...

> CSPs (MSFT, Meta, Google) are interested because they wouldn't want Nvidia/AMD/device vendors to provide different APIs for common telemetry access.

You realize I work for Meta, right?

Meta is interested in standardizing access to the data (specs) and having open source solutions to interact with the devices (in OpenBMC).  Having a library is perhaps a means to that end but not an end of itself.
Acknowledged

I think we need a legitimate discussion in the "alternatives" about the merits of this.  As written this is kind a sweeping generalization without any pro/cons expressed.

Which "device firmware stacks" are we attempting to target?  How do you know you're going to target them successfully?

I've asked for more details in the "APIs listed below" section but I'm not really getting a good picture of how much code we're really talking about here.  From my reading of the spec, we're proposing an entire library just to implement the encoding and decoding of the "Bulk Telemetry" command.  This should be like 20 lines of good C++ code.  At that point, the overhead we're spending here to even review this document, let alone create an entirely new [C] library with all the overhead of a "stable API", etc. just doesn't seem to justify this.  Just copy the code.  Someone could take the 3 pages of this spec and write this code for their platform in 2 hours.

Is there something I'm missing?

Probably a coincidence - Just an FYI - Intel has recently proposed Bulk telemetry proposal using the existing specs like PLDM Platform monitoring and control (dsp0248) + PLDM for file transfer (DSP0242) in DMTF, It's still in discussion, but that seems like a little better approach rather than building a new packet.

Was there any attempt by you guys to scale the pldm protocol for bulk telemetry ? what's the reason for building a new spec rather than improving what we already have ?

Aware of the same (we have also been involved in and contributed to those discussions). I am one of the authors of DSP0242.

It is not just about bulk telemetry and file IO though. PLDM T2 is not yet ready to be used across devices for all telemetry use-cases. Someday it will get there. Until then, the purpose of the OCP spec is to unify device telemetry protocols to run on top of MCTP with a common OCP header, which can be extended by vendors.

How do devices intend to version their protocol and commands?  Does OCP spec cover this?  What happens when version A of vendor hardware adds a command but version B modifies that command?

On OpenBMC, platform specific entity-manager configuration is expected.

The OCP spec does have an "OCP version" field. Vendor extensions can add their own command-specific versioning to denote modifications.

This would be the case (multiple apps or a generic app with an abstraction that requires vendor specific implementation) as long as there are commands that device vendors support that are not in a standard spec.
